nameStory: Seedbox gets its name from its distinctive cube-shaped seed pods that rattle when shaken, like nature's own dice box! The square pods are so perfectly geometric they look almost man-made, earning it the alternate name 'rattlebox' when the dried seeds shake around inside.
description: Seedbox is a wetland perennial that grows 2-4 feet tall with a bushy, upright habit. It produces cheerful yellow flowers with four rounded petals throughout the summer, followed by its trademark square-shaped seed pods. The plant has narrow, lance-shaped leaves that grow alternately up the stem, and thrives in marshy areas where its feet can stay wet.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Distinctive cube-shaped brown seed pods that are perfectly square when viewed from above - they rattle when shaken and feel papery and dry to the touch

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with exactly four rounded petals, about the size of a nickel, blooming in the leaf joints along the upper stem

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged alternately up the stem, smooth-edged and pointing upward at a slight angle

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Bushy perennial growing 2-4 feet tall with multiple upright stems that feel somewhat woody at the base

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Always found in wet areas - if your feet aren't getting damp, you're probably not looking at seedbox

habitat: Look for seedbox in marshes, wet meadows, swamps, and along the edges of ponds and slow streams throughout New England. It prefers areas with consistently moist or saturated soil and can tolerate seasonal flooding. You'll often find it growing alongside cattails, sedges, and other wetland plants in full sun to partial shade.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge from the wet soil, with narrow leaves unfurling alternately along the stems as they grow taller.
seasonality.summer: Bright yellow four-petaled flowers bloom continuously from mid-summer into early fall, appearing in the upper leaf joints.
seasonality.fall: The distinctive square seed pods mature to brown and begin rattling - this is the best time to confirm identification by the cube-shaped fruits.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems persist with dried square seed pods still attached, rattling in winter winds until spring growth begins anew.

funFact: The seed pods are so perfectly cube-shaped that they were once used as natural dice by some Native American groups - nature's geometry lesson that you can literally shake, rattle, and roll!
confusionNotes: The square seed pods make this plant nearly impossible to confuse with anything else once you've seen them. Before fruiting, the yellow four-petaled flowers might be confused with evening primroses, but those prefer drier habitats and have different leaf arrangements.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being in the evening primrose family, seedbox flowers stay open during the day unlike many of its relatives. The name 'water-primrose' can be confusing since it's not actually a primrose but gets the name from its family relationship.
compareHints: Seedbox stands out from its primrose-willow relatives by its cube-shaped fruits and alternate leaves - water purslane has opposite leaves and tiny flowers, while globefruit primrose-willow has round (not square) seed pods. The alternately arranged leaves are actually the key feature that gives this species its scientific name 'alternifolia.'

relatedSpecies.distinction: Water purslane differs from its Ludwigia relatives like seedbox and globefruit primrose-willow by its tiny, inconspicuous flowers and low, mat-forming growth habit.
Unlike its relative water purslane which has alternate leaves and tiny green flowers, globefruit primrose-willow has opposite leaves and yellow flowers.
